question: What does the GENIUS Act say about issuers, reserves and holder rights?
answer: The saved Act reading separates who may issue, what counts as a payment stablecoin, eligible backing, the interest ban, lawful-order duties and platform/size limits. The statutory provisions are not issuer approvals or proof of operation.

groups.label: What the Act's provisions say, in plain words

items.title: Who may issue
kv: Only a 'permitted payment stablecoin issuer' may issue a payment stablecoin in the United States. That means a U.S.-formed company that is (A) an approved subsidiary of an insured bank, (B) a federal qualified issuer (a nonbank or uninsured national bank approved by the OCC), or (C) a state qualified issuer.
It shall be unlawful for any person other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States. (Sec. 3(a))

items.title: Definition
kv: A digital asset used or designed for payment or settlement whose issuer is obligated to convert, redeem or repurchase it for a fixed amount of money and promises (or creates a reasonable expectation of) a stable value. National currencies, bank deposits and securities are excluded.
does not include a digital asset that— (i) is a national currency; (ii) is a deposit ...; (iii) is a security ... (Sec. 2(22)(B))

items.title: Reserves
kv: At least 1:1 reserves limited to: U.S. coins and currency; demand deposits; Treasury bills, notes or bonds with 93 days or less to maturity; money received under repurchase agreements backed by such Treasury bills; overnight reverse repurchase agreements collateralized by Treasuries; shares of registered government money market funds investing in these; other similarly liquid federal government assets the regulator approves; and tokenized forms of these. Reserves may not be pledged, rehypothecated or reused except in narrow cases. The issuer must publish its reserve composition monthly, and the month-end report must be examined by a registered public accounting firm.
Reserves required under paragraph (1)(A) may not be pledged, rehypothecated, or reused (Sec. 4(a)(2))

Clause (vi) is summarized from the quoted fragment 'securities issued by an investment company registered under section 8(a) of the Investment Company Act of 1940'; the full limits on which funds qualify were not re-read in this pass.

items.title: Interest ban
kv: Neither a permitted issuer nor a foreign issuer may pay a holder any form of interest or yield, in cash, tokens or anything else, solely for holding, using or keeping the coin. The ban names issuers; it does not name exchanges or other distributors. The OCC's March 2, 2026 proposed rule (not final) would presume the issuer is paying holders when it has an arrangement with an affiliate or related third party that pays them (proposed 12 CFR 15.10(c)(4), 91 FR 10202).

No permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer shall pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin. (Sec. 4(a)(11))
Whether the OCC presumption is rebuttable, and exactly how 'related third party' is defined, were not fully read; the CLARITY market-structure bill's reward limits have not become law.

sources.label: OCC proposed GENIUS rule (91 FR 10202), proposed 12 CFR 15.10(c)(4)

items.title: Lawful orders
kv: A 'lawful order' is one that requires a person to seize, freeze, burn or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins it issued. A permitted issuer may issue only if it has the technical ability to comply with such orders. A foreign issuer's coin may be offered in the U.S. only if the issuer can and will comply with lawful orders.
requires a person to seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins issued by the person (Sec. 2(16)(A))

items.title: Platform cutoff and size
kv: Starting three years after enactment (July 18, 2028), a digital-asset service provider may not offer or sell a payment stablecoin to a person in the United States unless a permitted issuer issued it (foreign issuers have a separate route). A state qualified issuer that passes the $10 billion outstanding threshold must move to the federal framework within 360 days unless its regulator grants a waiver.

beginning on the date that is 3 years after the date of enactment of this Act, it shall be unlawful for a digital asset service provider to offer or sell a payment stablecoin to a person in the United States, unless the payment stablecoin is issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer (Sec. 3(b)(1), assembled from quoted fragments)

The $10 billion figure is from the library's July 2026 cards; the fetched text of Sec. 4(d) referred to 'such threshold' without the number being quoted back. The foreign-issuer comparability provision is cited by the library as 12 U.S.C. 5916; its section number in the Act was not confirmed here. The Act's general effective date is kept in the genius_act_milestones master (January 18, 2027).

catalog_context.title: OCC final stablecoin rules: issuer duties, permissions and operating evidence
catalog_context.answer: The OCC's final GENIUS rule takes effect January 18, 2027. Its requirements attach to specific issuers, claims and custody relationships; approval, backing, capital, reporting and completed redemption require separate evidence.
